items.title: Charley Crockett Is Still Mad About Twin Temple, Says He ‘Lost Respect’ for Jack White
items.summary:
Charley Crockett has returned to a dispute most people had already filed away. In a long Instagram post published Aug. 18, the country singer disputed Twin Temple's claim that he removed the Los Angeles duo from shows over their satanic imagery, and took aim at Jack White, who booked the band after the story broke.

The original flare-up came more than a month earlier, when Twin Temple, who make Sixties-styled songs about the devil and the occult, said Crockett had cut them loose because of their act. The attention led to an opening slot with White and an appearance on The Daily Show. Crockett's response at the time was brief and jokey: "I thought they were like Black Sabbath, but they ain't. Not today, Satan."

In the new post, Crockett wrote that he decided about a month before the shows to drop the duo, first because their production requests were something "we couldn't accommodate them physically," and then because of what he saw of their stage show. "We told em the vibe just wasn't right for an all ages audience, and we paid em in full," he wrote. He accused the band and their team of engineering a statement "designed for effect" that made it look like a full tour had been cancelled rather than a couple of dates.

His sharpest words went to White. "[H]e used it to sell tickets too and I lost a lot of respect for him," Crockett wrote, adding that White and the White Stripes "purposely avoided political issues" two decades ago when "he needed all the help he could get." Rolling Stone, which reported on the post, noted that White released Icky Thump and has altered "The Big Three Killed My Baby" onstage to criticize George W. Bush and the Iraq War.

Crockett also faulted artists he said had praised him for years before using the episode to "kick me in the dick," and blamed the press, "save for one outlet," for ignoring the facts in what he called "the click bait traffic game that is America's left-right culture war." He accepted some blame as well: "It's my fault, I let em slip through and being that this here's my outfit, I'm the responsible party."

He closed defiantly, writing that he still shoots "from the hip" and that "real patriots think for themselves." Twin Temple, for their part, have not issued a new response to the post.

items.title: Cameron Winter Announces Live at Carnegie Hall
items.summary:
Cameron Winter will release his first live album, Live at Carnegie Hall, on October 9 through Partisan and PIAS. The record captures the Geese frontman's December performance at the venue, where he played pared-down versions of songs from his solo album Heavy Metal alongside three songs he had not previously released.

The Carnegie Hall date came during a short U.S. tour behind Heavy Metal, which Winter put out in 2024, a year before Geese released Getting Killed. The booking made him one of the youngest solo performers to headline the venue's Stern Auditorium.

Paul Thomas Anderson and Benny Safdie filmed the concert, though Pitchfork reported that no details about how or when that footage will be released have been shared. The album's inner sleeve shows Winter kissing Andrew Carnegie.

The tracklist runs eleven songs, opening with "It All Fell in the River" and closing with "Vines," and includes "Try as I May," "The Rolling Stones," "Cancer of the Skull," "Nina + Field of Cops," "$0" and "Take It With You."

items.title: Frank Beard, ZZ Top’s Hard-Shuffling Drummer, Dead at 77
items.summary:
Frank Beard, the drummer whose Texas shuffle anchored ZZ Top for more than five decades, died Monday at 77. Band representative Bob Merlis confirmed that Beard died in hospice care at his ranch in Richmond, Texas, surrounded by family. No cause of death was given.

"Today, Elwood and I lost a great friend and collaborator, and the world lost one of the most naturally innovative drummers and a great and true son of Texas," guitarist and singer Billy Gibbons wrote on social media. "His signature backbeat was key to keeping ZZ on top." The band cancelled shows in Salt Lake City on Aug. 18 and Colorado Springs on Aug. 19, and said the tour will resume this weekend in Austin.

Beard's health had been in question for some time. He underwent an emergency appendectomy in 2002 and stepped away from the band in 2025 for reasons that were never specified. Earlier this month ZZ Top scrapped a Hollywood Bowl date citing "insurmountable obstacles," which was later attributed to Beard's condition.

Born June 11, 1949 in Frankston, Texas, Beard came up through the Dallas scene, where he met bassist Dusty Hill and played with him in the Warlocks, American Blues and a counterfeit touring version of the Zombies. He joined Gibbons after ZZ Top's debut single "Salt Lick" and brought Hill along, completing the lineup that held for nearly fifty years. Recalling their first session in the 2019 documentary ZZ Top: That Little Ol' Band from Texas, Beard said, "I was jacked up on speed, so I made him jam for about eight hours til his tongue just fell out."

The band broke through with 1974's Tres Hombres, which reached the Billboard 200's Top 10 and carried "La Grange," followed by Fandango! and its Top 20 single "Tush." After 1976's Tejas the group paused, partly so Beard could get sober; he later spoke plainly about the cost, telling the documentary he sold his original Ludwig kit to buy drugs. ZZ Top returned in 1979 with Degüello and spent the following decade at a commercial peak with Eliminator, Afterburner and Recycler.

Rolling Stone, which reported his death, noted Beard's role as the band's steady center while attention went to the riffs and the beards he conspicuously did not wear. Speaking to the outlet in 1984, he credited manager Bill Ham with booking the group beneath fading headliners: "We did Mott the Hoople that way, Alice Cooper, Deep Purple. They were through, and they didn't care who knew it, so people would remember us."

items.title: Camp Flog Gnaw 2026 Lineup with Tyler, the Creator, Turnstile, and Steve Lacy
items.summary:
Tyler, the Creator has revealed the full lineup for Camp Flog Gnaw 2026, posting the names as a word jumble on the festival's website. The two-day event runs November 14th and 15th at the Dodger Stadium grounds in Los Angeles, the site it has used for most of its run.

Alongside Tyler, the bill includes Turnstile, Steve Lacy, Future, Lola Young, Don Toliver, Earl Sweatshirt, MIKE, Isaiah Rashad, Syd, Vince Staples, 2hollis, Not for Radio, Leon Thomas, Audrey Nuna, Magdalena Bay, JID, Lupe Fiasco, Quadeca, Wallows, Thee Sacred Souls, The Alchemist and Jane Remover.

Deeper on the lineup are 54 Ultra, Latin Mafia, Domo Genesis, Mike G, Casey Veggies, Natanya, Concrete Boys, Left Brain, threetwenty, Gabriel Jacoby, Liim, NSQK, Ama, 310babii, Nomi, GENA and Wyatt Waddell.

Tickets went on sale June 11th and sold out quickly, though the festival is running a waitlist through its site. According to Consequence, the festival is currently set to be Tyler, the Creator's only U.S. performance this year.

items.title: ‘Club Kid’ Trailer: Jordan Firstman Is A Messy Father In His Buzzy Directorial Debut
items.summary:
A24 has released the first trailer for Club Kid, the feature directing debut of Jordan Firstman, who also wrote the film and stars in it. The studio will open the movie in limited theaters starting Nov. 6.

Firstman plays a New York club promoter whose hard-partying life is interrupted when the 10-year-old son he didn't know about turns up. A24 acquired the film out of Cannes, reportedly outbidding several other buyers, after a premiere that drew a seven-minute standing ovation.

Deadline critic Damon Wise called it "an unlikely but still beautifully human story" and singled out Firstman's "elegant switch into a more serious tone, one that addresses all the questions you might have had about this man and his fitness to raise a kid."

Firstman told Deadline at Cannes that the film began as a joke about proximity: "My friends started having kids, and I was getting along with them in a funny way, and they would always laugh at me with kids." The script changed, he said, after a breakup from a partner he had partied with in Berlin. "I was just partying a lot myself and finding myself at this crossroads where the drugs were not hitting like they used to. But you keep doing them, and you're like, So they're not working, and I feel horrible for a week."

He added that the film keeps shifting for him: "I still learn new things about the film and myself every time I watch it." The November release puts Club Kid in the thick of awards season.
